questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to try living somewhere where the culture and academic environment were markedly different from those in Denmark. At the same time, I wanted to live in a place that made sense in relation to my studies and that I personally found exciting.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: none

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think SNU had created good guidelines that were easy to follow. Also, reading everything twice should make sure everything goes well.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There is an orientation evening that goes through the most important information. I was not in Seoul at the time, so I did not attend that evening, and I managed just fine anyway. The first week is mainly spent being introduced to your courses, for example if you want to drop a course and apply for a different one.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It will always be exciting to start in a new place where you are unfamiliar with the location, the systems, and the teaching structure. I found that many things work intuitively, and they use a system that is very similar to Absalon, which they call ETL. This is where everything is uploaded, including assignments, the syllabus, and preparatory materials.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I lived close to Sinchon Station, which is quite far from the university. I would recommend living off campus but closer to the university. Try to live near a metro station on Line 2 (the green line), as it makes it easy to get everywhere.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: From the beginning, I was determined not to live on campus. However, I am sure that if you want to be social with the other students, it is definitely worth trying to get a place there. That said, it is very popular and therefore quite difficult to secure a spot, and it is typically graduate students who get accommodation. I do not know enough about it, as I did not look into it myself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didnt interact with is so i dont know.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system for enrolling in courses is easy to use. However, it operates on a first-come, first-served basis, so there is a lot of competition for courses—make sure to have a Plan B. I was accepted into two of the courses that were my first priority, which meant I had to find three additional courses as backups. Therefore, make sure you have plenty of courses to choose from. I also recommend participating in the trial rounds so you become familiar with the system, as Korean students are used to it and you need to be quick on the keyboard.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Read above

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You will receive a guide along with all the other documents from the university. Read it carefully, and everything should be fine.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got 2 out of 5 courses that were my first priorities.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Overall, I had three courses that I was very satisfied with, and two where I felt the quality was weaker. This largely depends on which professor you get and how they structure their teaching. I also took two graduate-level courses, which are at a completely different level than undergraduate courses and therefore involved a heavier workload. Compared to the University of Copenhagen, the teaching structure felt somewhat more like a high-school system. Attendance is monitored, and class participation is recorded and counts toward your final grade.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Their teaching structure is somewhat similar to that of high school. They keep track of attendance, what you contribute in class, your attitude, assignments, midterms, presentations, and the final exam—all of which count toward the final grade you receive at the end

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Critical Communication Studies: The courses are really interesting, and you gain many insights into the contemporary world. I find it especially engaging when the material can be linked to real-world examples.

Art and science: I have a strong passion for art and have always been curious about it, so I thought it was a great way to explore another interest by taking a course on the subject. I learned a lot from it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: You can clearly feel the cultural differences between Denmark and South Korea, both in the way people communicate and in their body language. Many people are not very confident in English, so you often rely on gestures or translation apps. While I felt that Seoul became a home for me, I did not feel like part of the local population, as the cultural differences are quite significant

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: SNU buddy programme

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food, efficentcy, the city, museums, nature

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: I recommend applying for the ARC card outside the university, so make sure to print all the required documents in advance and submit them directly at the immigration office. Buy an eSIM—I got mine through the MobileMatter app. Also, get a Climate Card (their public transport card), which you can purchase at a convenience store. Finally, get a Revolut credit card. I recommend carrying two credit cards, as many places do not accept Apple Pay.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to explore Seoul out from the university!!! The city is amazing.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living far away from home and learning to integrate yourself into an opposite culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Socializing with strangers and doing group work in different ways.
